extracted.intended_audience: students and writers of the novel; literary critics and readers interested in fiction craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for composing and evaluating novels, with extended discussion of plot, endings, character/idea balance, and the fantastic. Draws on examples (Gide, Tristram Shandy, Beerbohm) to illustrate methods and risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (logical, intellectual aspect)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is the novel in its logical intellectual aspect: it requires mystery, the mysteries are solved later on; the novelist stands above his work, interested in cause and effect and giving an air of predetermination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat plot as a framework concerned with cause and effect and mystery. Be aware that plot-making positions the author 'above' the characters and may produce a sense of predetermination. Consider whether this logical framework is appropriate to the novel you want to write; recognize that a strictly prearranged plot can feel like a borrowed dramatic fetich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning vs organic growth (Should a novel be planned?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether a novel must be planned or whether it can grow: 'Why has a novel to be planned? Cannot it grow? ... cannot the novelist throw himself into it and be carried along to some goal that he does not foresee?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider allowing the book to develop organically rather than fixing every detail in advance. Modern approaches (e.g., Gide) attempt to replace rigid plotting with methods that permit reality or the material to 'dictate' to the author. Be aware that planning may be unsuitable for some types of novels; overplanning risks falseness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending / Conclusion coherence (sustained pep and truth to characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inherent defect of many novels is that 'they go off at the end' — explanations include failure of pep and the difficulty of reconciling characters who have 'been getting out of hand'. Death and marriage are often used as contrived ways to conclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid weak, bookish, or overly-logical conclusions that abandon the novel's flesh-and-blood truth. Maintain narrative energy ('pep') through to the end and resist relying on formulaic devices (death/marriage) merely to tie up plot threads. Preserve characters' integrity so the denouement feels earned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character autonomy vs authorial manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters may 'get out of hand', lay foundations and decline to build on them; the novelist may then 'labour personally' and pretend the characters are acting for him, mentioning their names and using inverted commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep characters alive as agents within the story rather than props to be forcibly bent into a prearranged plot. Avoid authorial intrusions that announce character actions as if staged; integrate character development so that outcomes emerge plausibly from the characters themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between human beings and non-human elements (ideas/themes)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two forces in the novel: human beings and 'a bundle of various things not human beings'; the novelist's business is to adjust these two forces and conciliate their claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek a workable reconciliation between character-driven material and the novel's non-human elements (ideas, themes, constructs). Do not allow themes or abstract 'bundles' to dominate to the detriment of believable human action, nor let characters entirely subsume thematic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader faculties required by plot-centred fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: For plot-centred works the reader must bring 'curiosity for the story, human feelings and a sense of value for the characters, intelligence and memory for the plot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plot fiction to engage these reader faculties: create curiosity, elicit empathy and value for characters, and construct a plot that rewards intelligence and memory. Failure to do so reduces reader investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy (definition and reader demand)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy 'asks us to pay something extra' — it compels an additional adjustment beyond accepting the book as a whole: the reader must accept certain impossible or odd things in the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing fantasy, anticipate that some readers will refuse the extra 'sixpence' of suspension required. Make the terms of the fantastic clear and internally consistent so readers who accept the initial condition can remain engaged rather than alienated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy devices (acceptable means of producing the fantastic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical devices used by fantastic writers include 'the introduction of a god, ghost, angel, monkey, monster, midget, witch into ordinary life; the introduction of ordinary men into no man's land, the future, the past, the interior of the earth, the fourth dimension; divings into and dividings of personality; parody or adaptation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices are limited in number but can be recycled freshly. Choose devices that suit your temperament and the book's tone; be inventive in application while maintaining suitability to the work's overall fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling, tone and mythology in fantasy
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful fantasy depends on handling: a mixture of realism, wittiness, charm and mythology; mythology is particularly important and 'supernatural machines' must be appropriately borrowed or created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the realistic and the mythic; select or invent mythological/supernatural elements that fit the book's voice. Poor handling can make the fantasy feel heavy or thin. Examples: Max Beerbohm's Zuleika Dobson uses a careful blend of mythology and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasy's relation to realism (supernatural present or suggested)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fantasy may either express the supernatural or merely suggest its absence/presence (e.g., Tristram Shandy suggests the supernatural without explicit apparitions); this produces a special effect and demands extra adjustment from readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to make the supernatural explicit or only implied. Both approaches can work, but be mindful of the general novel tone (often literal) — introducing the fantastic into a predominantly literal novel creates a distinct effect and may divide readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metafiction/self-insertion and mixing material
rubrics_metrics.description: An approach exemplified by Gide: include diaries, writer-characters and the author's impressions; 'Writers should mix themselves up in their material and be rolled over and over by it' rather than trying to subdue it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-insertion or metafictional devices to explore truth-in-life vs truth-in-art, but be wary of excessive solemnity. Such methods can be stimulating and repay careful study, yet carry risks (e.g., alienating readers or seeming self-indulgent) if not handled with balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't over-reason the subconscious / premature analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: A danger in attempting subconscious/subtle modes: reasoning 'so lucidly and patiently about the subconscious' can be ill-advised and may introduce mysticism at the wrong stage of the creative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with subconscious or fantastical material, allow it to arise organically in the writing rather than over-intellectualizing it during creation. Excessive analysis can drain the intended spontaneity and power of the material.
